content: A healthcare provider, also known as a health professional, refers to an organization or individual who delivers healthcare services in a systematic and professional manner to individuals in need. The National Library of Medicine (NLM) uses the term Health Personnel to describe men and women involved in providing health services, whether as independent practitioners or employees of health institutions and programs. This definition includes individuals regardless of their professional training or public regulation status. A hospital is a healthcare institution that often provides care for patients requiring longer-term stays. Modern hospitals are typically funded by the government, health organizations (both for-profit and non-profit), health insurance, charities, or donations. Historically, hospitals were often established and funded by religious orders or charitable individuals and leaders. Today, hospitals are staffed by professional physicians, surgeons, and nurses, whereas in the past, this work was commonly performed by members of religious orders or volunteers. A medical or clinical laboratory is a facility where biological specimens are tested to obtain information about a patient’s health. These laboratories are often divided into specialized departments, such as microbiology, hematology, clinical biochemistry, immunology, serology, histology, cytology, cytogenetics, and virology. In many countries, there are two primary types of laboratories: hospital laboratories, which perform tests for hospital patients, and private or community laboratories, which analyze samples from general practitioners, insurance companies, and other health clinics. Biomedical research, also known as experimental medicine or medical research, encompasses basic or applied research aimed at expanding knowledge in the field of medicine. This research is categorized into clinical trials, which evaluate the safety and efficacy of new treatments, and preclinical research, which focuses on developing new therapeutic strategies. Healthcare professionals include physicians, physician assistants, nurses, pharmacists, therapists, psychologists, veterinarians, dentists, optometrists, and other licensed or regulated individuals who provide various types of healthcare services. Among allied health personnel, physician assistants are sometimes referred to as physician extenders, according to the NLM. Advanced practice clinicians and mid-level providers are informal terms used to describe healthcare providers who are not physicians, such as nurse practitioners and physician assistants. In the United States, the number of advanced practice clinicians is growing at a faster rate than the number of physicians. These clinicians are capable of delivering intensive care comparable to that provided by medical trainees and can also provide hospital-based care similar to that of physicians. A mental health professional is an individual who provides services aimed at improving mental health or treating mental illnesses. This category includes psychiatrists, clinical psychologists, clinical social workers, psychiatric nurses, and other professionals. While these professionals often address similar illnesses, disorders, and conditions, their scope of practice varies significantly, primarily due to differences in education and training. A healthcare system refers to the organizational structure through which healthcare is delivered. Such systems may be managed or endorsed by governments or operated entirely or partially by private market-based institutions. Health insurance is a type of insurance in which the insurer covers the medical costs of the insured in cases of illness or accidents caused by covered factors. The insurer may be a private organization or a government agency. Market-based healthcare systems, such as the one in the United States, primarily rely on private health insurance.
